cumin.e: From Middle English comyn, from Old English cymen (which is cognate with Old High German kumin) and Old French cummin, both from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον…
cumin.x: Cumin is native to the region from the eastern Mediterranean to India.

cummerbund.e: Borrowed from Hindustani کمر بند / कमरबंद (kamarband), from Classical Persian کمربند (kamarband), from کمر (kamar, “waist”) + بند (band, “band”).
cummerbund.x: She saw dresses in every color of the rainbow; she saw lime green cummerbunds and pink cummerbunds and plaid ones.

cumulative.x: As for knowledge which man receiveth by teaching, it is cumulative, not original.

cuneiform.x: There, too, it was originally the vulgar script in contrast with the official cuneiform script employed for all official documents, compacts, etc.

cunning.e: From Middle English cunning, kunning, konnyng, alteration of earlier Middle English cunninde, kunnende, cunnand, from Old English cunnende, present participle of cunnan…
cunning.x: They are resolved to be cunning; let others run the hazard of being sincere.

cunningly.x: She was cunningly dressed in a black, sheer gown with gold ornaments showing her figure to perfection.

cupboard.e: Inherited from Middle English cuppeborde, cupbord. By surface analysis, cup + board.
cupboard.x: Put the cups back into the cupboard.

cupcake.x: “Listen, cupcake,” Cash tried to soothe. “Sometimes when grownups get mad, they say things they don't mean. I'm sure your mother—”

cupola.e: Borrowed from Italian cupola, from Latin cūpula (“little tub”); from Latin cūpa, cuppa (“cup”); named for its resemblance to a cup turned over. Doublet of cupula.
cupola.x: the light falling dimly through the foggy cupola.

curable.e: From Middle English curable, curabyll, from Old French curable. By surface analysis, cure + -able.

curative.x: The curative power of the antibiotics introduced in the 1950s was amazing at the time.

curator.e: From Latin cūrātor (“one who has care of a thing, a manager, guardian, trustee”), from cūrāre (“to take care of”), from cūra (“care, heed, attention, anxiety, grief”).
curator.x: Renowned curator Jacques Saunière staggered through the vaulted archway of the museum's Grand Gallery.

curdle.e: Metathesis of earlier dialectal cruddle, crudle, equivalent to curd + -le (frequentative suffix).
curdle.x: Too much lemon will curdle the milk in your tea.

curfew.e: From Middle English curfu, from Old French cuevre-fu (French couvre-feu), from the imperative of covrir (“to cover”) + fu (“fire”). Compare kerchief.
curfew.x: The city has been reported calm after a curfew was imposed.

curiosity.e: From Middle English curiosite, variant of curiouste, from Anglo-Norman curiouseté, from Latin cūriōsitātem, accusative of cūriōsitās. By surface analysis, curious + -ity.
curiosity.x: He put the strangely shaped rock in his curiosity cabinet.

curlew.e: From Middle English curlew, from Old French courlieu (see French courlis), claimed to be imitative of the bird's cry but apparently assimilated with dialectal *corliu…
curlew.x: That quivering wail from the billabong lying murkily mystic towards the East was only the cry of the fearing curlew.

curmudgeon.e: Numerous folk etymologies exist for this word. An alternative spelling attested in 1600 is cornmudgin, in Holland's translation of Livy, rendering Latin frūmentārius…
curmudgeon.x: There's a cranky curmudgeon working at the hospital who gives all the patients and other doctors flak.

currant.e: Borrowed from French raisin de Corinthe (literally “grapes of Corinth, the city in Greece”). Cognate with Dutch krent. Doublet of Corinth.

currency.x: Wampum was used as a currency by Amerindians.

cursive.e: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

cursor.e: Borrowed from Latin cursor (“runner”), from currō (“run”) + -or (agentive suffix). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European.

curtail.e: Alteration of curtal, from Old French courtault (“which has been shortened”), itself from court (“short”) (from Latin curtus) + -ault.
curtail.x: When the audience grew restless, the speaker curtailed her speech.

curtain.e: Inherited from Middle English curtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”), a calque from Ancient Greek.
curtain.x: He drew the curtains at 11:00pm before falling asleep.

curtsey.e: Variant of courtesy (1525) (from court + -esy), from Middle English curteisie, curtesie, from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie.
curtsey.x: "I’m sure you’ll excuse me, sir," said Mrs Varden, rising and curtseying.

curvaceous.e: From curv(e) + -aceous. Originally American English. First attested in the 1930s.
curvaceous.x: He watched her walk, upon curvaceous legs, to the edge of the bed. For just a second, she smiled down at him.

curvature.e: From Latin curvare, from Latin curvatura. See also curve. Displaced native Old English ġebīeġednes.
curvature.x: Constructional costs are kept to a minimum by the admissibility of heavy grades and sharp curvature.

curve.e: Attested since the 1690s, from Latin curvus (“bent, curved”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, curve, turn”) + *-wós.
curve.x: You should slow down when approaching a curve.

cuscus.e: From New Latin Cuscus, former genus name, ultimately (probably via French and Dutch koeskoes) from a local word for the marsupials in a language of the Moluccas.

cushion.e: From Middle English quysshyn, from later Old French coissin (modern coussin), from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) (with the…
cushion.x: Interest coverage is important because it is an indicator of how much cushion a company has in making its interest payments.

custodian.e: From a shortening of Latin custōdiānātus, from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”).
custodian.x: After their parents' death, their aunt became the children's custodian.

custom.e: PIE word *ḱóm PIE word *swé From Middle English custume, borrowed from Anglo-Norman custume, inherited from Latin consuētūdinem, a noun derived from cōnsuēscō, from con-…
custom.x: Much forbidden by elder custom is accepted today.

customary.e: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.
customary.x: The tenants are chiefly customary and heriotable.

customize.e: From custom + -ize. First attested in 1934 in American English.
customize.x: High-priced lattes and customized drinks helped lift the coffee chain’s US sales in the quarter ending on October 1, the company said Thursday.

customs.e: Plural of custom. Perhaps influenced by or taken as a corruption of customhouse, from Middle English custome hous.
customs.x: Customs of £200 were due on all the wine we took back from France.

cutaneous.e: From New Latin cutaneus, from Latin cutis (“skin”).

cuticle.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cutīcula (“cuticle, skin”). Doublet of cuticula.
cuticle.x: By that time she has pushed back his cuticles, cleaned his nails and painted them with clear polish.

cutie.e: A brand name of a particular cultivar of orange.

cutlass.e: From Middle French coutelas, from Old French coutel (“knife”) + -as (augmentative suffix).
cutlass.x: She could feel Tern’s stare fixed right between her shoulder blades, and knew he was aching to plunge his cutlass there.

cutler.e: From Middle English coteler (“knife-maker”), from Anglo-Norman cuteler, from Old French coutelier (“knife-maker”).

cutlery.e: From Middle English cotellerie, cutleri (“the cutler’s art or craft”), from Old French coutelerie (modern French coutellerie).
cutlery.x: Proper maintenance of your cutlery will keep the blades from dulling.

cutlet.e: From French côtelette (recorded in English since 1706), from Middle French costelette (“little rib”), from coste + -elette, from Old French coste (“rib, side”), from…

cutter.e: From Middle English cutter, cuttere, kutter. By surface analysis, cut + -er.
cutter.x: In some CNC programs, the diameter of the cutter (such as an end mill) is handled by cutter compensation codes.

cyanosis.x: She has real, real deep cyanosis around the eyes and mouth too.

cybernetic.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κυβερνητικός (kubernētikós, “good at steering, good pilot”), from κυβερνητική τέχνη (kubernētikḗ tékhnē, “the pilot’s art”), from Ancient…

cybernetics.e: From Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, guide, act as a pilot”) (whence English govern).

cyberpunk.e: From cyber- + -punk, coined by American writer and software developer Bruce Bethke as the title of a 1983 short story, and later popularized by Gardner Dozois.
cyberpunk.x: The film The Matrix redefined what a cyberpunk looked like.

cyberspace.e: Blend of cybernetics + space, equivalent to cyber- + space, coined by American-Canadian speculative fiction writer William Gibson in his short story collection Burning…

cyclamen.e: Borrowing from New Latin cyclamen, from Latin cyclamīnos.
cyclamen.x: An expectant mother would avoid cyclamen, stepping over it being an ominous sign.

cyclic.x: The weather had a cyclic pattern of rain and sun.

cycling.x: In all my years as a cycling fan, I've never seen a breakaway like this.

cycloid.x: In the firſt Courſe there was a Shoulder of Mutton, cut into an Æquilateral Triangle, a Piece of Beef into a Rhomboides, and a Pudding into a Cycloid.

cylinder.e: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive).

cylindrical.e: From Latin cylindricus + -al. By surface analysis, cylinder + -ical.

cynical.e: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al.
cynical.x: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received.

cytoplasm.e: Borrowed from German Zytoplasma, Cytoplasma. Equivalent to cyto- (“cell”) + -plasm (“contents of a cell”).

cytosine.e: After German Cytosin, equivalent to Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos) + -ine.
